Ying'an Tanhua owns the retained instruction: under Mingguo's gate there is no Chan to speak and no way to transmit — one sword only, and whoever it is, buddha or ancestor, saint or commoner, he lifts it and cuts; turn your body over under that blade-edge and you may leave one cloister and enter another and squeeze the old man on the seat — see the mouth still dripping and sling your satchel and walk: is it not a joy? and he closes with Shending Yan's word — the seeking must be real seeking, the waking real waking; King Yama has no patience for much talk.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie. Juelang Daosheng owns the retained close: when sky lightens and the sun is bright, lead out that broken-horned iron ox and ride it tumbling head over tail away: is it not a joy? — a shout, down from the seat; before it, the whole address plays the good-news turn — coming is a fine mountain, sitting, staying, going a fine mountain, only you look up and see no sky.

Senses.Explanation: Is it not a joy: the laugh after the master's tread, the satchel slung under the blade, the iron ox ridden into daylight — one exclamation poured over a finished picture. Ying'an Tanhua, instructing the monk Zhan: under Mingguo's gate there is no Chan to speak, no way to transmit — one sword only; whoever comes, buddha or ancestor, saint or commoner, lift and cut; turn your body under that edge and you may leave one cloister for another and squeeze the old man on the seat — see the mouth still dripping, sling the satchel, walk: is it not a joy? Yuanwu Keqin, before the assembly: watch the ancients seal the news at an elder's word — Shuilao, taken by one of Mazu's treads, rose and roared laughing: a hundred thousand gates, an ocean of meanings, all recognized at the root of a single hair-tip — is it not a joy? and on to Linji's sixty blows and the rice-gruel plainness before Dayu. Liao'an Qingyu, at the new year: the three-age buddhas cannot say it, the six founders cannot transmit it, the old abbots under heaven cannot see it — last night the seat-leader and store-keeper said it all, and the mountain monk won a mouthful of rice; if I eat, are you filled? one line here that fuses holy and common: is it not a joy? else — one song sung to green hills, a feeling the white clouds never know. Linquan Conglun, closing the Zhaozhou knowing-or-not commentary: should you arrive at both upright and slant, principle and working in accord, no long road to bog you — stroll the bird-path, be a free-and-easy patched monk: is it not a joy? were it not for Zhaozhou's own pointing, the parting peril would cost the traveler his toll. Miyun Yuanwu, re-raising Deshan: a peerless decree, held up beyond the rule — a good hand; this old monk is otherwise: the moment he says 'a man of Silla' — out on a linked string of blows, make him a free-and-easy patched monk: is it not a joy? Wunian You, to the general: turn your head back quickly, make the hubbub itself your resting place — tea and rice, waking and dreaming, delight and vexation, lift it moment on moment and finish the ten-thousand-age affair in this one life: is it not a joy? fear only that rank passes fast and the year's last day stands at the door. Juelang Daosheng, seeing the visitors off: it is all a fine mountain — coming, sitting, staying, going; only you look up and see no sky; when sky lightens and the sun is bright, lead out the broken-horned iron ox and ride it tumbling away: is it not a joy? — a shout, down from the seat.
